Display Quality Control: the Grayscale Standard Display Function, AAPM TG18, and QA Programs

Unit 2: Clinical Engineering. Lesson 13 of 65 in CIIP Academy.

A radiologist says a diagnostic monitor "looks washed out" on the second screen. The images are fine. Displays drift, and only measurement tells you by how much.

Why calibrate

Human perception is the reason: the eye judges small brightness steps along a curve, and the display must follow that curve so equal steps in the data look equal on screen.

The grayscale standard display function (DICOM part 14) maps each pixel value to a luminance so equal steps look equally different. That is perceptual linearization. A calibrated display shows the same contrast wherever it is used.

What gets tested

AAPM test patterns (TG18, replaced by TG270) support these checks:

Check                 Tolerance
Ambient light         20 to 40 lux
Maximum luminance     at least 250 cd/m2 (350 or more common for primary reads)
Contrast ratio        above 250 diagnostic, above 100 clinical
Contrast response     within 10 percent of the GSDF
Uniformity            corners and center within 30 percent
Matched displays      centers within 10 percent of each other

Also resolution, noise, and geometric patterns, and pixel dropouts.

Acceptance versus routine

A qualified medical physicist (QMP) usually runs acceptance testing, often with a test pattern or a phantom, an object built to image in a known way.

An acceptance test is done once at installation with the full set. Routine QC follows on a schedule with simpler checks and a visual pattern.

Automation and records

Calibration software with a built-in photometer can adjust displays and report remotely. A QA program names who performs each test, how often, and where records are kept. A medical physicist or trained team signs off. Mammography displays need a qualified medical physicist before clinical use.

Exam tip: a clean-looking image proves nothing about a display. Test pattern plus meter is the evidence, and each test result is documented.
Remember
Diagnostic displays are calibrated to the grayscale standard display function and checked with test patterns and a meter, with acceptance testing once and routine QC on a schedule.
Deeper explanation

Display Quality Control: the Grayscale Standard Display Function, AAPM TG18, and QA Programs, explained slowly

An acceptance test and a routine test

The same device is tested differently over its life. Keep the tests separate in the plan.

Check                   Acceptance (once)           Routine (scheduled)
Pattern set             full set                    simpler checks, visual pattern
Luminance               measured with a meter       measured or from the built-in sensor
Contrast response       compared to the GSDF        compared to the GSDF
Uniformity              four corners and center     usual check
Noise pattern           low-contrast dots           check
Internal sensor         compared with external      compared every 10,000 backlight hours
Sign-off                physicist                   physicist or trained team

Worked example of a luminance check

A diagnostic display must reach at least 250 cd/m2 maximum luminance, and the contrast ratio is maximum divided by minimum luminance. The meter reads a maximum of 380 and a minimum of 1.2. The ratio is 380 / 1.2, about 317, which is above the 250 needed for a diagnostic display. A clinical review display only needs above 100.

Now check uniformity: the four corners read 360, 375, 355, and 380, and the center reads 380. The largest difference is 380 minus 355, which is 25. As a percent of 380 that is 6.6 percent, within the 30 percent tolerance.

Check two displays at one workstation: centers read 380 and 335. The difference is 45, and 45 / 380 is 11.8 percent, which exceeds the 10 percent allowance for matching displays. Recalibrate one of them.

Remote monitoring

Calibration software reads the built-in photometer, adjusts each display, and reports results to a central console. That lets the PACS team see which displays are out of tolerance without visiting each room. A report is a record, so keep it.

Who signs

For most diagnostic displays a medical physicist or a trained and supported team signs the acceptance. For mammography, a qualified medical physicist is required before clinical use. The PACS team keeps the records, the schedule, and the failed-display list.

Do not trust the eye

A display can drift for months with no visible fault. A clean image is not a test, and a complaint from a reader is a reason to measure, not a reason to adjust by eye.
